title: Robust Federated Inference
one_liner: Combine predictions from many local models without sharing the models themselves, while staying accurate even when some model outputs are attacked or corrupted.
lead: Federated prediction systems let several local models keep their data and internal settings private while a server combines only their output scores. This is attractive for cross-organization deployment, but it opens a new attack surface: an adversary can corrupt some model outputs and make the final vote fail. This paper studies that setting directly. It shows when simple averaging is naturally stable because honest outputs stay close and the winning class keeps a clear margin, then builds a stronger nonlinear aggregator based on DeepSets plus attack-aware training and a test-time defense step.

problem.h2: Why federated prediction is easy to attack
paras: A central server may ask several local models for class scores and then combine them. If all local models are honest, averaging can work well. But a few corrupted clients can push the final combined score toward the wrong class, especially when the honest models already disagree. That means privacy-preserving collaboration can fail at the last step: combining outputs.

The paper points out that training-time and test-time defenses from ordinary adversarial learning do not transfer automatically. Here the attacker may only need to change a few client outputs, not the whole input example. The aggregation rule itself must therefore be studied as a defense object.

callout.html: Treat the server-side combiner as the defense target: analyze when averaging survives, then train a stronger set-based combiner that resists corrupted client outputs because it can downweight suspicious output patterns.

panels.title: 1. Several local models answer one query
panels.viz_args: Hospitals, phones, or companies keep their own models but send output scores to one server.
panels.caption: The server sees predictions only, not the underlying data or model weights.

panels.title: 2. Some outputs are corrupted
panels.caption: A small number of bad outputs can overturn the final decision when honest models are not well aligned.

panels.title: 3. Check whether averaging is enough
panels.viz_args: If honest outputs are close and the top class has a wide margin, averaging can still survive.
panels.caption: Simple averaging is not hopeless, but it needs favorable conditions.

panels.title: 4. Learn a stronger set combiner
panels.caption: A learned combiner can recognize suspicious output sets and reduce their impact.

panels.title: 5. Private collaboration stays useful
panels.caption: The server can combine local expertise without letting a few bad outputs dominate.

steps.text: Each local model sends its class scores for the same input example.
Study when the average stays correct based on honest-model agreement and the winning-class margin.
Learn a set-based server model that reads the collection of client outputs without caring about their order.

steps.b: 4. Include attack-aware training and test-time filtering
steps.text: Expose the combiner to attacked output sets during training and apply a defense step when making predictions.
Use the defended combiner output as the federated system's prediction.

paras: The paper changes the unit of defense from the client model to the server-side aggregation rule. That matters because a federated system may not control or inspect each local model deeply, but it always controls the final combiner. By defending the combiner directly, the method can improve the whole system even when the local models remain untouched.
object.object: the server-side rule that combines local prediction sets

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: honest disagreement margin
hidden.name: how far the honest clients separate the correct class from the nearest wrong class
paras: The server rarely knows which clients are corrupted. What it can observe is the spread of client outputs. The most important hidden quantity is the honest disagreement margin: if honest clients mostly agree on the correct class and place it far above the next class, an attacker must work much harder to flip the final answer. If honest clients are split already, only a small push may be enough.

This quantity matters for both parts of the paper. It explains when simple averaging already survives, and it tells the learned set combiner what kind of output sets should be trusted or treated as suspicious.

heat.caption: Darker cells show the conditions that decide whether corrupted outputs can overturn the combined prediction.

reads.html: If the honest clients are already close to a common answer, the server has room to ignore a few strange votes. If they disagree a lot, the server is fragile.

The theory links aggregation error to honest-response dissimilarity and the margin between the top two classes, then uses a set-based model to improve decisions under attack because the server can read the whole output set instead of averaging every client equally.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: learn patterns over sets of client outputs
paras: Averaging treats every client output the same. That is good when all outputs are honest and similarly noisy, but bad when a few outputs are attacked. A DeepSets combiner can do more. It reads the whole set of client outputs and learns patterns such as "most clients agree, but a small group is sharply inconsistent." That helps because the server can reduce the impact of suspicious outputs instead of letting them shift the average directly.

Attack-aware training matters because the combiner must see corrupted sets during learning, otherwise it has no reason to distinguish them from natural client disagreement. The extra test-time defense step helps again because attacks at deployment may not look exactly like the attacked sets used in training. Combining both stages keeps the server more stable across different attack patterns.

stages.s: A set of class-score outputs from many local models
Measure agreement and margin under average-based rules
Feed the whole set into a DeepSets combiner
Train and defend against corrupted output sets
A more attack-resistant final class decision

math.words: Final class score = output head applied to the sum of per-client transformed scores
symbols: the class-score vector from client i
the per-client transformation used by the set combiner
order-free pooling over all client outputs
the server head that converts the pooled summary into the final class score

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose five honest clients favor class A and two corrupted clients push class B strongly.
If plain averaging sums all seven outputs equally, class B may win when the honest margin is small.
A trained set combiner can map the five mutually consistent outputs to a strong pooled summary and map the two inconsistent outputs to a smaller contribution.
After pooling, the server head still gives class A the highest final score.
The gain comes from learning which output patterns look trustworthy across the whole set, not from inspecting one client alone.

math.note: The form is order-free, which fits the federated setting because the server should care about the set of outputs, not about which slot each client occupied.

charts.title: Plain averaging under attack
charts.note: Equal treatment of all clients fails when a few corrupted outputs are far from the honest group.

charts.title: DeepSets plus two-stage defense
charts.note: The learned set combiner helps because it can identify inconsistent client-output patterns and reduce their influence.

items.b: Honest clients may disagree for valid reasons.
items.html: If local models are trained on very different data, their outputs can naturally vary a lot. The server may then mistake honest diversity for an attack because both look inconsistent.
A server trained on one family of corruptions can still be surprised by a very different corruption strategy because attack-aware training never covers every possible manipulation.

items.b: Too many clients may be corrupted.
items.html: If the corrupted share is large enough, even a good set combiner may fail because the honest group no longer forms the dominant pattern in the output set.
The method is strongest when most clients are honest and the honest group has a visible class margin, because then the combiner has a real signal to protect.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small federated image or text classifier with several local models and one server. First measure clean accuracy and attacked accuracy under simple averaging. Then replace the server with a DeepSets combiner trained on attacked output sets and add the paper's test-time defense step. The demo should compare how often the final prediction flips under different numbers of corrupted clients. The defended combiner should keep more correct predictions because it learns when a subset of client outputs is inconsistent with the honest majority.

A useful interface would also show the client score sets for several examples. Watching a few extreme outputs fail to dominate the final answer makes the server-side defense easier to understand than a single accuracy table.
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows that privacy-preserving collaboration is only practical if the final combiner stays stable when some participating outputs are malicious.
